body_markdown:
One of my favorite hats is starting to show its age. Things like hats aren’t meant to last forever, and especially not if they serve their purpose. This one certainly has—and it’s got the stains to prove it.


How we spend our days leaves its signature on the things we wear, and those signs accumulate faster when our hands carry not only sweat, dirt, and the occasional blood, but also the grease and grime of machines. I wrote last week about signs that confirm[you own a project car](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/5-signs-you-own-a-project-car/) , one of which is that you own two sets of clothes: regular clothes, and clothes for working on your car. Rolling around on a garage floor, or the driveway, or street, has a way of tearing your favorite shirt or pants into tatters. Such clothes are both annoying and a strange sign of honor. As “chicks dig scars” seemed to encourage boys of a certain age to do a bunch of dumb things and pick scabs for a week after, having a separate set of clothes for garage work somehow encourages me to be even rougher on them.


You can’t fake the marks of the old-car lifestyle. I put them on this hat, and I have the stories to prove it. Funny enough, I didn’t go looking for this hat: Twelve or thirteen years ago, a friend traveled to a motorcycle event on the West Coast in the depth of Michigan winter and upon his return dropped a crisp tan trucker hat on my desk. For a while, the hat hung in the basement, because I felt weird wearing a hat from an event I didn’t go to. Time softened my stance, and before long the hat was in the regular rotation.


You can tell I’m right-hand dominant when putting this hat on or taking it off.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


The sweat stains are starting to grow but are hardly bad. Shows I have air conditioning in my home shop for sure.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


The bill might be starting to separate from the rest, but not yet.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


The hat is a promotional piece for a Yamaha motorcycle program called Yard Built designed to encourage custom builds on a couple of its then-new bikes. The program is long gone, but that doesn’t bother me: I never much cared about the graphic Yamaha stitched onto the hat, especially after I started wearing it. I’ve left my own identifying factors: Each readjustment of the bill after investigating a leaking transmission or handling a grimy suspension bit left another little mark, all of which combined into a dark spot on the bill. It’s the polar opposite of the stickers inside the bills of hats to highlight how fresh and new they are.


Look at that fresh hat, still unstained and new.


Kayla Shreeves


Nearly exactly 10 years ago!


Kayla Shreeves


The hats, pants, and shirts in our closet are not much different than the cars in our garage: What gets worn, and more specifically worn out, reveals the gap between who we are and who we’d like to be. A few years ago, ahead of New Year’s Day, I resolved to use my KTM 950 Adventure S until at least one piece wore out. Until something truly needed to be addressed, I wouldn’t work on or “upgrade” the machine. (Regular readers will know exactly how much of a challenge this is for me.) The resolution reflected a desire to do more—and to do less. My success has been mixed: While I’ve ridden the bike more than usual this summer, I haven’t yet worn out anything more than a set of tires.


My 1930 Model A Ford has fared better (or worse, depending on your flavor of mechanical sympathy). It has brand-new tires, but the 2021 date code on those unworn tires shows that I’m just not someone who daily-drives an antique car in the summer, as I imagined when I installed those tires and brakes. What have I been doing instead? That well-worn Yamaha hat tells the true story: I’m someone who can’t stop fixing broken things.


The post[The Things We Wear—and Wear Out](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/mechanical-sympathy/the-things-we-wear-and-wear-out/) appeared first on[Hagerty Media](https://www.hagerty.com/media) .
